messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elijah stood at the edge of a client’s living room, his brush hovering over a freshly primed wall. His PCL-5 score of 67 reflects the severity of a presentation that began when his younger brother Isaiah collapsed at a neighborhood barbecue, and by the time the paramedics arrived, Elijah had already knelt beside a chest that no longer answered. The shock of that sudden stillness rewired his nervous system, and now the distant wail of an ambulance cutting through his street immediately locks his shoulders, forcing his breath shallow as his body braces for impact. When that sound reaches him, the image of Isaiah’s final, peaceful face surfaces unbidden, pulling a wave of grief so heavy it steals his air. Elijah tells himself he cannot continue this work, convinced that the accident had permanently dismantled his life and left him set apart from everyone who still believes in tomorrow. This conviction that his future is ruined dictates his nights, ensuring he sleeps only in fits, his body locked in a permanent state of readiness even inside his own bedroom. He scans the corners of the house for any sign of approaching crisis, a habit that makes him hyperaware of the neighborhood, so that a neighbor’s tearful retelling of a recent funeral instantly pulls his focus outward. When the fear peaks, it leaves him with a hollow, imageless dread that somehow feels more real than any picture, a sensation that reinforces his belief that he no longer knows who he is beneath the fear. The more he fears the loss of his old self, the more he expects danger to arrive unannounced, which keeps his shoulders drawn up and his breath shallow whenever he steps onto a scaffold or passes a hospital driveway. His wife notices how he withdraws, how the quiet of their marital bed has been replaced by restless pacing that leaves him exhausted before dawn. He avoids discussing Isaiah’s death, fearing that speaking the words will shatter the fragile calm he has managed to construct, yet the very act of hiding deepens his isolation, feeding the ruminations that keep him mentally chained to the moment of the collapse. Over weeks, this cycle has become his architecture: the vivid flashbacks keep his nervous system permanently on alert, which in turn convinces him that his identity is fractured and his life is beyond repair. That hollow dread then pushes him to avoid any workplace that mirrors the trauma, steering him away from ladders and drop cloths. Meanwhile, the night vigilance bleeds into his waking hours, fragmenting his focus and spawning more visual memories of the collapse. His constant state of alert at home makes him scan every passing street corner for emergency vehicles and every casual conversation for the cadence of mourning, which tightens the loop. His paint can no longer hold his focus; the job that once grounded him now feels like a minefield, and his contractor has noticed how he leaves early when a radio picks up emergency broadcasts. He has come to believe that his body is a trap, constantly firing alarms at nothing, but also that he deserves the exhaustion because he failed to save Isaiah. Now, at fifty-five, he sits in his therapist’s office with calloused hands clenched around his knees, hoping someone can teach him how to breathe again. What frightens him most is the prospect of returning to the scaffold, of facing the open sky and the weight of a life that feels permanently broken. He wants to wake up without scanning the ceiling for danger, to hear a siren without his muscles seizing, and to remember his brother without feeling like the ground has given way beneath him. He is ready to stop running from the quiet, even if it means facing the storm he has spent months trying to outrun.
